chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: Getting Goosby's party into McElroy's ballroom
summary: Fields advises Goosby on how to demand admission, and Pops McElroy admits his party free.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, this stuff that we can't go and I know you can tell them to let us in, we have our money and we got to break down this

junk and I said I'm for it, but you know what I wish you would do, why don't you get your bunch together and anybody that's playing, when one of these country and western bands are playing, come up and tell them that you want to come in and then lay down your money; but I said you want to break in when I'm coming, don't you know how they're going to treat that. Pops McElroy won't want no more negro bands in then.
Yeah, he just wouldn't hire any black bands.

That's it exactly. And so he finally acknowledged, he finally saw the point that I was talking about, so after he saw that, I said, I'll tell you what, we seem to be together now and I think Pops McElroy is okay, I said I'm going to talk to him and not only will I see that you get in, but you can get in, you and your party and won't have to pay a penny. Well, all right, but that won't mean anything unless we--I said that's all right, what it means, but I'm going
to see that you get in the dance, so you bring them on down.

So then I spoke to Pops McElroy and told him that my friend from Oklahoma was down and he wanted to bring a party in, I said I don't know how many they are. Pops McElroy said bring in whoever you want.

So Dewey came on down, brought his party, I think four or five of them, but everybody was nice and happy and then I finally told Pops what he said and he said well, I'm with him, but you told him exactly right. He said what they need to do is come anything, when I got any band, they don't have to wait until I have a negro band, when I have anybody come on down and demand admission to the thing and he said then we will get this thing straight-ened out.
And so everything was happy and he went on out after the dance and we parted,
Dewey Goosby, from Enid, Oklahoma originally and during World War II he was out working in the shipyard.
Where is Dewey now; is he still living?
I frankly don't know, but I know a few years back he was, because he came back to Oklahoma.
